chapter: The jazz war with Leonard Feather
title: Feather and Ulanov attack Hodes and the moldy figs
summary: Hodes says Leonard Feather and Barry Ulanov made him a focal point of attacks on traditional jazz. Pee Wee Russell and Louis Armstrong also took shots.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: This is the hateful thing that it's hard to forgive, that these few handful of writers, starting with Leonard
Feather and Barry Ulanov, who was fixing Leonard's coattails, so to speak, and then a few more that followed in their footsteps because they seemed like winners. And this is what--
They seemed to -- Leonard particularly seemed to vent his spleen on you, as sort of symbolic of everything that they called the moldy figs.
Yes. Well, I had the Jazz Record magazine.
You were getting a lot of exposure.
A lot of exposure. Many Village people -- I had many so-called fans and people that really dug me and liked me, personally and musically.

So he made me a focal point, but not only me alone. Somewhere -- I read somewhere where he talked about Louis Armstrong's music being -- should have gone out with button shoes and Pee Wee Russell caught it from him. And this is one of the things that happened. Some of the musicians either didn't want to see what was happening, or wouldn't look at what's happening, as long as it wasn't happening to them.
Some of the traditional musicians. And not -- but Muggsy Spanier was not one of them. He read it loud and clear.
